title: Ankita Konwar Becomes First Assamese Woman to Cross the English Channel, Learned to Swim Just Three Years Ago
excerpt: The endurance athlete and wife of fitness icon Milind Soman completed the iconic Dover-to-Calais crossing as part of an international relay team, marking the 100th anniversary of the first woman's Channel swim.
body:
• Ankita Konwar became the first Assamese woman and first woman from Northeast India to cross the English Channel, completing the Dover-to-Calais relay swim in 13 hours and 5 minutes on July 3.
  • Konwar only learned to swim three years ago, and has since completed a Full Ironman in Barcelona and the T100 Triathlon in Dubai.
  • The crossing was officially recognized by the English Channel Swimming Association and coincides with the 100th anniversary of Gertrude Ederle's historic 1926 Channel swim.
  • Konwar credited husband Milind Soman and coach Arjun Kawle for their support, and pledged to attempt a solo crossing in the future.

From Non-Swimmer to Channel Crosser

Three years ago, Ankita Konwar could not swim. On July 3, she stood on the French coast after crossing one of the world's most demanding open-water routes — the English Channel — becoming the first Assamese woman and first woman from Northeast India to complete the crossing.

Konwar finished the iconic Dover-to-Calais swim as part of a six-member international relay team, battling freezing water temperatures, powerful currents and unpredictable tides over 13 hours and 5 minutes. The relay began at 1:30 AM and concluded at 2:35 PM London time. The English Channel Swimming Association, which governs official Channel crossings, has formally recognized the achievement.

""She was the first woman in the world to have done it."

""She was the first woman in the world to have done it."

A Centenary Crossing

The timing carries its own significance. Konwar's swim came during the centenary year of Gertrude Ederle's historic 1926 feat — when the American swimmer became the first woman to cross the English Channel solo, completing it in 14 hours and 34 minutes and beating the existing men's record by nearly two hours.

"What makes it even more special is that it's the 100th year celebration of Gertrude Ederle crossing the channel," Konwar wrote on Instagram after the swim. "She was the first woman in the world to have done it. And in 2026, I became the first Assamese woman to have crossed it in a relay, with a promise of a solo one day to myself."

"The English Channel is far more than a swim — it's a journey of resilience, teamwork and trusting yourself when nature tests every ounce of your spirit."

— Ankita Konwar

A Rapid Rise in Endurance Sports

Konwar's trajectory from complete beginner to Channel swimmer in just three years is remarkable by any standard. After learning to swim, she quickly moved into competitive endurance events, completing a Full Ironman triathlon in Barcelona — a grueling 3.86-kilometer swim, 180-kilometer bike ride and 42-kilometer marathon — and competing in the elite T100 Triathlon in Dubai.

The Channel swim came after she recovered from an injury earlier this year, adding another layer of difficulty to her preparation. Her coach Arjun Kawle guided her through the recovery and training.

"I'm so proud of the girl in me who decided to learn how to swim three years ago," she wrote. "She and I have come a long way since then."

Family Support and What's Next

Konwar is married to Milind Soman, the actor, model and ultramarathon runner who has become one of India's most prominent fitness advocates. She credited him as "the biggest support a partner can ask for" in her post-swim message.

"Carrying the Indian flag while representing Assam and the Northeast is an honour I will cherish forever," she said. "If someone like me, who wasn't even a swimmer once, can stand here today, then anything is possible with consistency and courage."

The relay crossing is not the end of Konwar's Channel ambitions. She has publicly committed to attempting a solo crossing — swimming the 33-kilometer stretch entirely on her own, without a wetsuit as Channel rules require, through water temperatures that can drop below 15°C. If successful, it would place her among a small number of Indian women to complete the feat solo.
